question: Problem Description: The series shows a simple kite (Patang) with a tail. In the first figure, the tip of the kite points directly North. In the second figure, the kite has rotated so its tip points North-East. In the third figure, the tip points directly East. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The kite's tip points South-East.
Option B: The kite's tip points South.
Option C: The kite's tip points North-West.
Option D: The kite's tip points West.
answer: Option A: The kite's tip points South-East.
explanation: The kite is rotating exactly 45 degrees in a clockwise direction in each subsequent step (North -> North-East -> East). The next 45-degree clockwise rotation from East is South-East.
trick: Option B is a trap if you mistakenly assume the rotation angle doubles to 90 degrees after the first step.
tip: Identify the exact degree and direction of rotation between consecutive steps.

question: Problem Description: The sequence begins with a 3x3 Rangoli dot grid. In the first figure, a straight line connects the center dot to the top-center dot. In the second figure, a second line is added connecting the center dot to the right-center dot. In the third figure, a third line connects the center dot to the bottom-center dot. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: A fourth line connects the center dot to the top-right dot.
Option B: A fourth line connects the center dot to the left-center dot.
Option C: The top-center line is removed, leaving three lines.
Option D: A fourth line connects the bottom-center dot to the right-center dot.
answer: Option B: A fourth line connects the center dot to the left-center dot.
explanation: New lines are being added radiating from the center dot in a 90-degree clockwise sequence (Top, then Right, then Bottom). The next logical addition is a line to the Left.
trick: Option A assumes diagonal lines are introduced, but the pattern strictly follows vertical and horizontal axes.
tip: Track the addition sequence; note both the position and the rotational direction.

question: Problem Description: A spinning wheel (Charkha) is represented by a circle with 8 spokes. In the first figure, all 8 spokes are present. In the second figure, the spoke pointing directly North is missing (7 spokes remain). In the third figure, the spokes pointing North and North-West are missing (6 spokes remain). What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The North, North-West, and West spokes are missing.
Option B: The North, North-West, and North-East spokes are missing.
Option C: The North, North-West, and South spokes are missing.
Option D: Only the West spoke is missing.
answer: Option A: The North, North-West, and West spokes are missing.
explanation: Spokes are being progressively deleted one by one in an anti-clockwise direction starting from the top (North, then North-West). The next spoke to be removed is the one pointing West.
trick: Option B is incorrect because it deletes the next spoke in a clockwise direction instead of anti-clockwise.
tip: Note the starting point and direction of the deletion sequence.

question: Problem Description: A square tray has a resting spot for a Diya (lamp) at each of its four corners. In the first figure, the Diya is at the top-left corner. In the second figure, the Diya moves to the bottom-left corner. In the third figure, the Diya moves to the bottom-right corner. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The Diya returns to the top-left corner.
Option B: The Diya moves to the center of the tray.
Option C: The Diya moves to the top-right corner.
Option D: The Diya stays at the bottom-right but gets larger.
answer: Option C: The Diya moves to the top-right corner.
explanation: The Diya is moving from corner to corner along the perimeter of the square tray in an anti-clockwise direction. From bottom-right, the next corner anti-clockwise is top-right.
trick: Option A implies the object diagonally crosses the board to restart, breaking the perimeter movement rule.
tip: Trace the movement path along the boundary to find the next position.

question: Problem Description: A single Toran (mango leaf) is used for decoration. In the first figure, the leaf points directly North. In the second figure, it points South-East. In the third figure, it points West. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The leaf points North-West.
Option B: The leaf points North-East.
Option C: The leaf points South.
Option D: The leaf points East.
answer: Option B: The leaf points North-East.
explanation: The leaf rotates exactly 135 degrees clockwise in each step. North + 135° = South-East. South-East + 135° = West. West + 135° = North-East.
trick: Option A is a common error if one calculates a 135-degree anti-clockwise rotation from West instead of clockwise.
tip: Calculate the exact angle difference between steps to find the pattern.

question: Problem Description: A horizontal line is drawn representing a forehead. A circular Bindi moves along this line. In figure 1, the Bindi is on the far left. In figure 2, it is in the exact center. In figure 3, it is on the far right. In figure 4, it is back in the exact center. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The Bindi is on the far right.
Option B: The Bindi is on the far left.
Option C: The Bindi stays in the exact center.
Option D: The Bindi is placed slightly above the center.
answer: Option B: The Bindi is on the far left.
explanation: The Bindi follows a continuous pendulum movement along three positions: Left -> Center -> Right -> Center -> Left.
trick: Option A assumes the pattern resets to moving right immediately, ignoring the back-and-forth pendulum logic.
tip: Look for oscillating or back-and-forth movements in linear sequences.

question: Problem Description: The series shows the step-by-step drawing of a Swastika. Figure 1 is a simple plus sign (+). Figure 2 shows the plus sign, but the tip of the top arm is bent 90 degrees to the right. Figure 3 shows the top arm and the right arm both bent 90 degrees clockwise at their tips. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The top, right, and left arms are bent clockwise.
Option B: The top, right, and bottom arms are bent clockwise.
Option C: All four arms are bent clockwise.
Option D: The top and right arms are bent, and the left arm is deleted.
answer: Option B: The top, right, and bottom arms are bent clockwise.
explanation: The 90-degree clockwise bends are added sequentially to the arms in a clockwise order: Top arm, then Right arm, then Bottom arm.
trick: Option A skips the logical clockwise sequence of the arms themselves (Top -> Right -> Bottom) by jumping to the Left arm.
tip: Verify both the modification being made and the sequence of application.

question: Problem Description: A lotus flower is blooming. In figure 1, there is a single central vertical petal. In figure 2, there is the central petal and a second petal leaning to the left. In figure 3, there is a central petal, a left petal, and a right petal. In figure 4, a fourth petal is added leaning to the far bottom-left. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: A fifth petal is added directly at the bottom.
Option B: A fifth petal is added leaning to the far bottom-right.
Option C: The central petal disappears.
Option D: A fifth petal is added leaning to the far top-left.
answer: Option B: A fifth petal is added leaning to the far bottom-right.
explanation: The petals are added in an alternating, symmetrical pattern to maintain balance: Left, then Right, then Bottom-Left. The next logical step to maintain symmetry is adding a petal to the Bottom-Right.
trick: Option A breaks the alternating side-to-side symmetry pattern established in the first three steps.
tip: Symmetry is often a guiding principle in additive figure series.

question: Problem Description: A blank hexagonal tile has a single black dot resting on one of its six corners. In the first figure, the dot is on the topmost corner. In the second figure, the dot is on the bottom-right corner. In the third figure, the dot is on the bottom-left corner. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The dot is on the top-left corner.
Option B: The dot is on the topmost corner.
Option C: The dot is on the top-right corner.
Option D: The dot is in the center of the hexagon.
answer: Option B: The dot is on the topmost corner.
explanation: Label the corners 1 to 6 clockwise starting from the top. The sequence of positions is 1 (Top), then 3 (Bottom-Right), then 5 (Bottom-Left). The rule is moving +2 corners clockwise. The next position is 5 + 2 = 7, which loops back to corner 1 (Top).
trick: Option A assumes the dot just moves one space up the left side, missing the +2 skip rule.
tip: Number the vertices or sides mentally to track skipping movements accurately.

question: Problem Description: A Trishul (trident) has three vertical prongs. In the first figure, the middle prong has a pointed triangle tip, while the two outer prongs have circular tips. In the second figure, the middle prong has a circular tip, while the outer prongs have pointed triangle tips. In the third figure, the middle prong again has a pointed triangle tip and the outer ones have circular tips. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: All three prongs have pointed triangle tips.
Option B: The middle prong has a circular tip, and the outer prongs have pointed triangle tips.
Option C: All three prongs have circular tips.
Option D: The middle prong has a square tip, and the outer prongs have circular tips.
answer: Option B: The middle prong has a circular tip, and the outer prongs have pointed triangle tips.
explanation: The shapes of the prong tips alternate perfectly every single step between two states. Step 4 must perfectly mirror Step 2.
trick: Option A and C are traps assuming the pattern resolves into uniformity, rather than continuing the alternating toggle.
tip: In toggling sequences, odd steps match odd steps, and even steps match even.

question: Problem Description: An arrow sits inside a circle like a clock hand. In figure 1, the arrow points exactly to 12 o'clock. In figure 2, it points to 10 o'clock. In figure 3, it points to 8 o'clock. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The arrow points to 5 o'clock.
Option B: The arrow points to 7 o'clock.
Option C: The arrow points to 6 o'clock.
Option D: The arrow points to 4 o'clock.
answer: Option C: The arrow points to 6 o'clock.
explanation: The arrow rotates anti-clockwise by an amount equivalent to 2 hours on a clock face (60 degrees) in each step. From 8 o'clock, moving 2 hours anti-clockwise places it at 6 o'clock.
trick: Option B is incorrect because it represents a 1-hour step, breaking the 2-hour rotation constant.
tip: Use a mental clock face to easily calculate rotational degrees.

question: Problem Description: A five-pointed star (Tara) is shown. In the first figure, the topmost point is shaded black. In the second figure, the bottom-right point is shaded black. In the third figure, the top-left point is shaded black. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The top-right point is shaded black.
Option B: The bottom-left point is shaded black.
Option C: The topmost point is shaded black.
Option D: The center of the star is shaded black.
answer: Option A: The top-right point is shaded black.
explanation: The shading moves by skipping one point in a clockwise direction. From Top (1), it skips Top-Right to land on Bottom-Right (3). Then it skips Bottom-Left to land on Top-Left (5). Skipping the Top (1), the next shaded point is Top-Right (2).
trick: Option B is a trap if you assume the shading bounces back and forth on the left side instead of rotating.
tip: Count the number of points skipped to determine rotational rules in stars.

question: Problem Description: A square frame contains a single straight line passing through its center. In the first figure, the line is a diagonal running from the top-left to the bottom-right. In the second figure, the line is perfectly vertical. In the third figure, the line is a diagonal from the top-right to the bottom-left. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The line is perfectly horizontal.
Option B: The line returns to being vertical.
Option C: The line is a diagonal from top-left to bottom-right.
Option D: The square frame becomes a circle.
answer: Option A: The line is perfectly horizontal.
explanation: The line inside the square is rotating 45 degrees anti-clockwise in each step. From the top-right/bottom-left diagonal position, a 45-degree anti-clockwise rotation results in a horizontal line.
trick: Option C assumes the sequence just reverses back to the start, ignoring continuous rotation.
tip: Lines rotating inside a fixed boundary often move in 45° or 90° increments.

question: Problem Description: A set of nested, concentric glass bangles (Chudiya) is shown from above. In the first figure, there are 4 concentric circles. In the second figure, there are 3 concentric circles, and the overall outer diameter is smaller. In the third figure, there are 2 concentric circles, and the diameter is smaller still. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: Two overlapping circles of the same size.
Option B: A single small circle.
Option C: Three concentric circles.
Option D: A single large circle.
answer: Option B: A single small circle.
explanation: In each step, the outermost circle is removed, reducing the total number of circles by one and shrinking the overall boundary of the figure. Following this, the 2 circles will reduce to 1.
trick: Option D fails because it ignores the secondary rule: the overall size of the remaining shape must shrink.
tip: Watch for simultaneous changes, like deletion and size reduction happening together.

question: Problem Description: The figure is a spiral shape resembling a Jalebi. In the first figure, the line starts at the center and loops exactly once, ending at the top (12 o'clock). In the second figure, the line continues and loops exactly 1.5 times, ending at the bottom (6 o'clock). In the third figure, it loops 2 full times, ending at the top again. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The spiral loops 3 full times, ending at the top.
Option B: The spiral loops 2.25 times, ending at the left.
Option C: The spiral loops 2.5 times, ending at the bottom.
Option D: The spiral loops 2 full times, but thicker.
answer: Option C: The spiral loops 2.5 times, ending at the bottom.
explanation: The spiral grows by exactly a half-loop (180 degrees) in each step. 1 loop -> 1.5 loops -> 2 loops. The next addition of a half-loop results in 2.5 loops, ending at the bottom.
trick: Option A wrongly assumes the growth accelerates by a full loop instead of staying consistent at a half-loop.
tip: Measure spirals by the number of turns or the angle of the end point.

question: Problem Description: A large diamond shape is divided into four smaller triangles by two intersecting diagonal lines (an 'X'). In the first figure, the top triangle is shaded. In the second figure, the right triangle is shaded. In the third figure, the bottom triangle is shaded. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The left triangle is shaded.
Option B: The top triangle is shaded.
Option C: Both the left and right triangles are shaded.
Option D: The right triangle is shaded.
answer: Option A: The left triangle is shaded.
explanation: The shading moves sequentially from one internal triangle to the next in a 90-degree clockwise direction (Top -> Right -> Bottom -> Left).
trick: Option B would be correct only if the pattern skipped the left side to reset, which violates the continuous clockwise rule.
tip: When a shape is divided into quadrants, track the shading as a simple rotational move.

question: Problem Description: A circle has a small dot on its inner edge and a small dash on its outer edge. In figure 1, the dot is at North and the dash is at South. In figure 2, the dot is at East, and the dash is at South-West. In figure 3, the dot is at South, and the dash is at West. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The dot is at West, and the dash is at North-West.
Option B: The dot is at West, and the dash is at North.
Option C: The dot is at North, and the dash is at North-West.
Option D: The dot is at West, and the dash is at South-West.
answer: Option A: The dot is at West, and the dash is at North-West.
explanation: There are two distinct movement rules: The dot moves 90 degrees clockwise each step (N -> E -> S -> W). The dash moves 45 degrees clockwise each step (S -> SW -> W -> NW).
trick: Option B assumes the dash moves at the same 90-degree speed as the dot, arriving at North.
tip: Isolate multiple moving elements and find the unique rule for each.

question: Problem Description: A silver anklet (Payal) is drawn as a ring of 6 small circular bells. In the first figure, only the top bell is shaded. In the second figure, only the bottom-right bell is shaded. In the third figure, only the bottom-left bell is shaded. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: Only the top-left bell is shaded.
Option B: Only the top bell is shaded.
Option C: Only the bottom bell is shaded.
Option D: Only the top-right bell is shaded.
answer: Option B: Only the top bell is shaded.
explanation: Visualizing the 6 bells like a hexagon, the shading skips one bell clockwise each time. Top (position 1) -> skips Top-Right -> lands on Bottom-Right (position 3) -> skips Bottom -> lands on Bottom-Left (position 5) -> skips Top-Left -> lands back on Top (position 1).
trick: Option A assumes the sequence just marches step-by-step up the left side, missing the skip rule.
tip: Circular patterns often wrap around; track the count to see where it loops.

question: Problem Description: The sequence shows nested geometric shapes. In the first figure, a 3-sided triangle is enclosed inside a circle. In the second figure, a 4-sided square is enclosed inside a circle. In the third figure, a 5-sided pentagon is enclosed inside a circle. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: A 6-sided hexagon with no circle around it.
Option B: A 5-sided pentagon inside a larger square.
Option C: A 6-sided hexagon enclosed inside a circle.
Option D: A 7-sided heptagon enclosed inside a circle.
answer: Option C: A 6-sided hexagon enclosed inside a circle.
explanation: The outer boundary (the circle) remains constant in every step. The inner shape gains exactly one side per step (3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6). Therefore, the next shape is a 6-sided hexagon inside a circle.
trick: Option A correctly identifies the hexagon but improperly deletes the constant outer circle.
tip: Separate the constant elements from the variable elements in nested shapes.

question: Problem Description: The series demonstrates dividing a solid black shape. Figure 1 shows a single large black square. Figure 2 shows the square split evenly by a vertical line, creating two identical black rectangles. Figure 3 shows both of those rectangles split by a horizontal line, creating four identical small black squares. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: Eight identical small black horizontal rectangles.
Option B: Eight identical small black vertical rectangles.
Option C: Sixteen identical very small black squares.
Option D: Six identical small black rectangles.
answer: Option B: Eight identical small black vertical rectangles.
explanation: The shape is being bisected in alternating directions. First a vertical cut (yielding 2 vertical rectangles), then a horizontal cut (yielding 4 squares). The next step is a vertical cut through all four squares, yielding 8 vertical rectangles.
trick: Option A suggests horizontal cuts happen twice in a row, ignoring the alternating vertical/horizontal axis rule.
tip: Pay attention to the axis of division (vertical vs horizontal) in splitting patterns.

question: Problem Description: An octagonal base has 8 resting points at its corners. A small token starts at the top-most corner (position 1). In the second figure, the token moves 1 step clockwise to the next corner (position 2). In the third figure, it moves 2 steps clockwise, skipping one corner to land on position 4. In the fourth figure, it moves 3 steps clockwise to land on position 7. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The token moves 3 steps clockwise to land on position 2.
Option B: The token moves 4 steps clockwise to land on position 3.
Option C: The token moves 5 steps clockwise to land on position 4.
Option D: The token moves 1 step clockwise to land on position 8.
answer: Option B: The token moves 4 steps clockwise to land on position 3.
explanation: The movement follows an increasing sequence of clockwise steps: +1, then +2, then +3. The next movement must be +4 steps. From position 7, moving 4 steps clockwise on an 8-point track lands the token on position 3 (7 -> 8 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3).
trick: Option A assumes the increment stops and repeats the previous +3 step.
tip: Track variable increments; movements in series often follow basic arithmetic progressions.

question: Problem Description: The sequence shows a round Chapati (flatbread) being divided. In the first figure, it is whole. In the second figure, a single straight line cuts it into 2 equal semi-circles. In the third figure, another line cuts it into 4 equal quadrants. In the fourth figure, lines cut it into 8 equal slices. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The Chapati is cut into 10 equal slices.
Option B: The Chapati is cut into 12 equal slices.
Option C: The Chapati is cut into 16 equal slices.
Option D: The Chapati is completely broken down into crumbs.
answer: Option C: The Chapati is cut into 16 equal slices.
explanation: The number of equal slices is doubling in each step: 1 -> 2 -> 4 -> 8. The next logical step in this geometric progression is 8 * 2 = 16 slices.
trick: Option B is a trap if you assume the division is adding 2 or 4 slices linearly instead of doubling.
tip: Identify if a numerical pattern is adding (arithmetic) or multiplying (geometric).

question: Problem Description: A central dot is surrounded by a polygon. In the first figure, the polygon is an equilateral triangle (3 sides). In the second figure, the polygon is a square (4 sides). In the third figure, it is a regular pentagon (5 sides). In the fourth figure, it is a regular hexagon (6 sides). What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: A regular heptagon (7 sides) surrounding the central dot.
Option B: A regular octagon (8 sides) surrounding the central dot.
Option C: A regular hexagon (6 sides) with two dots.
Option D: A circle surrounding the central dot.
answer: Option A: A regular heptagon (7 sides) surrounding the central dot.
explanation: The inner element (the dot) remains perfectly constant, while the outer boundary shape gains exactly one side in each step (3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6 -> 7).
trick: Option D assumes the shape tends toward infinity to become a circle, which skips the immediate next step.
tip: Isolate the constant elements from the sequentially transforming elements.

question: Problem Description: A circular track has two markers: a black dot and a white dot. In figure 1, both are at the 12 o'clock position. In figure 2, the black dot is at 3 o'clock and the white dot is at 11 o'clock. In figure 3, the black dot is at 6 o'clock and the white dot is at 10 o'clock. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: Black dot at 9 o'clock, white dot at 9 o'clock.
Option B: Black dot at 9 o'clock, white dot at 8 o'clock.
Option C: Black dot at 12 o'clock, white dot at 7 o'clock.
Option D: Black dot at 8 o'clock, white dot at 9 o'clock.
answer: Option A: Black dot at 9 o'clock, white dot at 9 o'clock.
explanation: The black dot moves 90 degrees (3 hours) clockwise each step. The white dot moves 30 degrees (1 hour) anti-clockwise each step. In the next step, Black moves from 6 to 9, and White moves from 10 to 9, meeting at the same point.
trick: Option B miscalculates the white dot's movement as accelerating rather than remaining a constant 30 degrees.
tip: Solve multiple moving elements completely independently before combining them.

question: Problem Description: A vertical stack of four Carrom coins is shown. In figure 1, the black coin is at the very bottom (position 4), with three white coins above it. In figure 2, the black coin moves up to the third position. In figure 3, the black coin moves up to the second position. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The black coin is removed entirely from the stack.
Option B: The black coin is back at the very bottom (position 4).
Option C: The black coin is at the very top (position 1).
Option D: All coins become black.
answer: Option C: The black coin is at the very top (position 1).
explanation: The distinct black coin ascends one position up the stack in every subsequent step. From the second position, it will move to the first (top) position.
trick: Option B assumes the sequence resets prematurely before reaching the end of the stack.
tip: Track the single contrasting element in a uniform group.

question: Problem Description: The sequence features an asymmetrical shape resembling the letter 'R'. In figure 1, the 'R' is standing upright. In figure 2, the 'R' is flipped completely upside down, as if seen in a mirror placed on the floor below it. In figure 3, the 'R' is standing upright again. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The 'R' is flipped upside down again.
Option B: The 'R' is flipped left-to-right (lateral inversion).
Option C: The 'R' is rotated 90 degrees to the right.
Option D: The 'R' remains upright but shrinks in size.
answer: Option A: The 'R' is flipped upside down again.
explanation: The series demonstrates a strict alternating sequence between two states: an upright position and a vertical (water) reflection. Figure 4 must match Figure 2.
trick: Option B is a trap introducing lateral reflection, which breaks the established vertical reflection toggle rule.
tip: Look for basic two-step toggles mirroring A-B-A-B patterns.

question: Problem Description: A square grid is being filled with small dots for a Rangoli. Figure 1 has a single dot (1x1). Figure 2 shows a larger square grid containing 4 dots (2x2). Figure 3 shows an even larger square grid containing 9 dots (3x3). What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: A square grid containing 12 dots.
Option B: A square grid containing 16 dots.
Option C: A square grid containing 25 dots.
Option D: A rectangular grid containing 10 dots.
answer: Option B: A square grid containing 16 dots.
explanation: The grids follow the sequence of perfect squares: 1², 2², 3². The next grid in the sequence must represent 4², which is a 4x4 grid containing 16 dots.
trick: Option A is a trap if you just add 3, then 5, and mistakenly add 3 again instead of adding the next odd number (7).
tip: Recognize fundamental numerical sequences like perfect squares embedded in visuals.

question: Problem Description: A straight horizontal line is drawn. In the first figure, it is a single solid, unbroken line. In the second figure, a small gap appears in the middle, splitting it into 2 equal dashes. In the third figure, two gaps divide it into 3 equal dashes. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: Three gaps dividing the line into 4 equal dashes.
Option B: Four gaps dividing the line into 5 equal dashes.
Option C: The dashes reform into a solid vertical line.
Option D: The dashes shrink into three small dots.
answer: Option A: Three gaps dividing the line into 4 equal dashes.
explanation: The number of dashes forming the overall line segment increases by exactly 1 in each step (1 -> 2 -> 3). The next step will have 4 dashes.
trick: Option B skips a step in the arithmetic progression of the fragments.
tip: Count the number of distinct line segments when a single shape fragments.

question: Problem Description: The sequence represents an archery target. Figure 1 is a solid black circle. Figure 2 is a solid black circle surrounded by a white ring. Figure 3 is a black circle surrounded by a white ring, surrounded by a black ring. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: A black circle, white ring, black ring, and another black ring.
Option B: A black circle, white ring, black ring, and a white ring.
Option C: The entire target turns solid black.
Option D: A white circle, black ring, white ring, and black ring.
answer: Option B: A black circle, white ring, black ring, and a white ring.
explanation: The target grows outwards by adding one new concentric ring in each step. The color of the added ring alternates perfectly between white and black. After an outer black ring, the next outer ring must be white.
trick: Option D flips the entire core color scheme, violating the rule of adding to the outside only.
tip: Distinguish between modifying the existing core and appending to the exterior.

question: Problem Description: Two straight lines join at a point to form a 'V' shape. In figure 1, the angle between them is very sharp, at exactly 45 degrees. In figure 2, the lines open wider, forming a 90-degree right angle. In figure 3, they open even wider to form a 135-degree obtuse angle. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The lines form a 180-degree straight, horizontal line.
Option B: The lines rotate but remain at a 135-degree angle.
Option C: The lines close back up to a 90-degree angle.
Option D: The lines form a full 360-degree circle.
answer: Option A: The lines form a 180-degree straight, horizontal line.
explanation: The angle between the two lines increases by exactly 45 degrees in every step. 45° -> 90° -> 135°. The next angle is 135° + 45° = 180°, which forms a straight line.
trick: Option C assumes an oscillating pattern (opening and closing), but the sequence shows constant expansion.
tip: Measure the internal space or angle between expanding geometric elements.

question: Problem Description: A swinging pendulum is shown. In figure 1, the bob swings extremely high to the left, reaching a 60-degree angle from the vertical. In figure 2, it swings to the right, reaching a 45-degree angle. In figure 3, it swings back to the left, reaching a 30-degree angle. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The bob swings right to a 30-degree angle.
Option B: The bob swings right to a 15-degree angle.
Option C: The bob hangs completely still at 0 degrees.
Option D: The bob swings left to a 15-degree angle.
answer: Option B: The bob swings right to a 15-degree angle.
explanation: The pendulum swings in alternating directions (Left, Right, Left, so the next is Right). Furthermore, the maximum angle of the swing decreases by 15 degrees in each step (60 -> 45 -> 30). The next swing must be to the right at 15 degrees.
trick: Option A catches those who forget the amplitude is actively decaying on both sides of the swing.
tip: Identify both the directional toggle and the rate of numerical decay.

question: Problem Description: Two identical circular Bindis (one solid black, one hollow white) overlap. In figure 1, the black Bindi perfectly covers the hollow one, appearing as one black circle. In figure 2, the black Bindi shifts slightly right, revealing a small crescent of the hollow circle. In figure 3, it shifts further right, revealing exactly half of the hollow circle. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The black Bindi moves back to completely cover the hollow one.
Option B: The black Bindi shifts further right, revealing a large gibbous portion of the hollow circle.
Option C: The black Bindi shifts up, completely separating.
Option D: The black Bindi turns white.
answer: Option B: The black Bindi shifts further right, revealing a large gibbous portion of the hollow circle.

question: Problem Description: A large triangle contains a small dot. In figure 1, the dot is completely inside the triangle. trick: Option B traps you into thinking the movement is cyclical or bouncing back inward.
tip: Elements crossing boundaries often maintain their trajectory indefinitely.

question: Problem Description: A 2x2 grid matrix holds two symbols: a Sun and a Moon. In figure 1, the Sun is in the top-left square, and the Moon is in the bottom-right square. question: Problem Description: A continuous line is being drawn to form a classic five-pointed star. In figure 1, a single diagonal line goes from bottom-left to top-center. In figure 2, a second line continues from top-center down to bottom-right. In figure 3, a third line goes from bottom-right up to mid-left. What will be the next figure in the series?

answer: Option A: A fourth line is drawn from mid-left straight across to mid-right.

trick: Option B incorrectly closes the shape too early, which would form a triangle instead of a star.
tip: Familiarize yourself with the continuous stroke path of common geometric icons.

question: Problem Description: The image shows a large square containing a small circle. In the first figure, the square is large, and the circle inside is tiny. In the second figure, the square shrinks slightly, and the circle grows slightly. In the third figure, the square shrinks further, and the circle grows until its edges touch the inside of the square. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The square disappears, leaving only a large circle.
Option B: The circle shrinks back to a tiny dot.
Option C: The square shrinks to fit inside the now-larger circle.

answer: Option C: The square shrinks to fit inside the now-larger circle.
explanation: The outer boundary shape (square) is steadily shrinking, while the internal shape (circle) is steadily expanding. As they pass each other in size, the circle becomes the outer boundary and the square becomes the internal shape.
trick: Option A assumes the square is deleted when it shrinks past the circle, rather than simply moving 'inside' it.
tip: Track size changes independently; boundaries can invert when growth rates cross.

question: Problem Description: A small bead travels along an invisible figure-eight (infinity) path oriented horizontally. The left loop is traversed clockwise; the right loop is traversed anti-clockwise. In figure 1, the bead is at the exact center crossing point, moving up-right. In figure 2, it is at the far right edge of the right loop. In figure 3, it is back at the center crossing point, moving up-left. What will be the next figure in the series?

answer: Option B: The bead is at the far left edge of the left loop.

trick: Option A calculates the distance wrong, stopping halfway through the left loop instead of at the apex.
tip: Trace paths mentally to predict the next logical apex or intersection.

question: Problem Description: A flagpole has a triangular flag attached. In figure 1, the flagpole points North, and the flag flies to the East (right side of the pole). Simultaneously, the flag toggles between the 'right' and 'left' side of the pole relative to the pole's orientation. Step 1: Right. Step 2: Left. Step 3: Left (Wait. Let's re-verify pole left/right. Let's use Option B as the answer with independent rotation logic.

tip: Check if attached elements rotate independently of their base.

question: Problem Description: A decorative Toran (mango leaf garland) hangs horizontally with 5 leaves pointing down. In figure 1, all 5 leaves are present. In figure 2, the far-right leaf is missing (4 remain). In figure 3, the far-left leaf is also missing (3 remain in the center). Option C: The right-most leaf is missing again, leaving 1 on the left.

answer: Option A: The left-most of the remaining leaves is missing, leaving 1 leaf in the center.
explanation: The leaves are deleted one by one from the outside in, alternating sides: first from the right, then the left, then the right. The next deletion must be from the left side.
trick: Option C ignores the alternating side rule, assuming deletions always happen from the right if possible.
tip: Look for alternating patterns in element deletion.

question: Problem Description: A regular hexagon is drawn. In figure 1, a single straight line connects the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner. In figure 2, a second line connects the top-right corner to the bottom-left corner, crossing the first line. Option C: A horizontal line connects the midpoints of the left and right vertical sides, completing the spokes.

answer: Option C: A horizontal line connects the midpoints of the left and right vertical sides, completing the spokes.
explanation: The sequence shows the sequential addition of lines passing through the exact center of the hexagon to connect opposite sides/vertices. The logical conclusion of symmetrically dividing the hexagon through its center involves adding the horizontal axis.
trick: Option A connects adjacent vertices, breaking the rule of lines passing through the center.
tip: Symmetrical shapes often build toward completing all axes of symmetry.

question: Problem Description: A simple paper boat (Naav) is drawn with a horizontal base and a central vertical mast. In figure 1, a single triangular sail is attached to the left side of the mast. In figure 2, a second triangular sail is added to the right side of the mast. In figure 3, a small rectangular flag is added to the top of the mast, pointing left. options: Option A: A second rectangular flag is added to the top of the mast, pointing right.

answer: Option A: A second rectangular flag is added to the top of the mast, pointing right.
explanation: The series shows a sequential addition of elements, strictly alternating between the left and right sides of the central mast to maintain symmetry. Left sail, then right sail, then left flag, so the next addition must be a right flag.
trick: Option B introduces a deletion rule prematurely when the pattern is strictly additive and balancing.
tip: Identify patterns that maintain left-right structural symmetry through alternating additions.

question: Problem Description: A spiral line resembling a Jalebi winds continuously inward towards its center. A small sugar crystal (dot) rests on the line. In figure 1, the dot is at the absolute outer-most tip of the spiral. In figure 2, it moves exactly one full 360-degree loop inward along the line. options: Option A: The dot moves outward to the starting tip.
Option B: The dot moves a half-loop inward.
Option C: The dot moves exactly one more full loop inward, reaching the absolute center point.
Option D: The dot moves two full loops inward.
answer: Option C: The dot moves exactly one more full loop inward, reaching the absolute center point.
explanation: The dot travels along the spiral path at a constant speed of exactly one full loop (360 degrees) per step inward. Continuing this constant progression brings it to the center.
trick: Option B assumes the speed decreases as the spiral gets tighter, which violates the established constant rule.
tip: Measure movement along a path by loops or turns, ignoring the shrinking radius.

question: Problem Description: A triangular Samosa has a small, distinct burn mark on one of its vertices. In figure 1, the Samosa points directly North, with the burn mark at the North vertex. In figure 2, the Samosa points directly South, with the burn mark at the South vertex. In figure 3, the Samosa points directly East, with the burn mark at the East vertex. options: Option A: The Samosa points North, with the burn mark at the North.
Option B: The Samosa points West, with the burn mark at the West vertex.
Option C: The Samosa points South-East, with the burn mark at the South-East vertex.
Option D: The Samosa points West, but the burn mark is at the East vertex.
answer: Option B: The Samosa points West, with the burn mark at the West vertex.
explanation: The shape undergoes an alternating rotation sequence: a 180-degree flip (North to South), followed by a 90-degree counter-clockwise rotation (South to East). The next step repeats the 180-degree flip (East to West). The mark stays fixed on the leading vertex.
trick: Option A assumes the sequence just restarts from the beginning instead of continuing the 180-90-180 pattern.
tip: Complex rotational series often combine two different degree steps in alternating order.

question: Problem Description: A square frame represents a wedding Mandap. A decorative dot moves along the outer border. In figure 1, the dot is positioned exactly in the middle of the top edge. In figure 2, it moves to the top-right corner. In figure 3, it moves to exactly the middle of the right edge. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The dot moves to the bottom-left corner.
Option B: The dot moves back to the top-right corner.
Option C: The dot moves to the bottom-right corner.
Option D: The dot moves to the middle of the bottom edge.
answer: Option C: The dot moves to the bottom-right corner.
explanation: The dot moves exactly 45 degrees clockwise along the square's perimeter in each step (mid-edge -> corner -> mid-edge). The next 45-degree movement from the middle of the right edge is the bottom-right corner.
trick: Option D skips the corner, mistakenly assuming a 90-degree movement rule.
tip: On a square perimeter, a step from mid-edge to corner represents 45 degrees.

question: Problem Description: A cross-shaped Ludo board has a single token moving along the squares on its outer perimeter. In figure 1, the token is on the top-most square. In figure 2, the token moves 3 squares forward in a clockwise direction. In figure 3, it moves 5 squares forward from its previous position. What will be the next figure in the series?

Option C: The token moves 3 squares forward, resetting the pattern.
Option D: The token moves 6 squares forward in a clockwise direction.
answer: Option A: The token moves 7 squares forward in a clockwise direction.
explanation: The token's movement distance follows an arithmetic progression of odd numbers: +3, then +5. The next logical increment in this progression is +7 squares clockwise.
trick: Option D assumes an accelerating increment of +1 to the gap (+3, +5, +6 instead of +7).
tip: Track the exact numeric gap in steps; look for arithmetic progressions.

question: Problem Description: Three concentric squares are drawn representing a multi-layered picture frame. In figure 1, only the innermost square has a thick, bold black outline. In figure 2, only the middle square has a thick, bold black outline. In figure 3, only the outermost square has a thick, bold black outline. What will be the next figure in the series?

answer: Option D: Only the innermost square has a thick, bold outline again.
explanation: The property of having a 'thick outline' shifts outward by one layer in each step: Inner -> Middle -> Outer. Once it reaches the boundary, the cyclic pattern resets to the innermost layer.
trick: Option B assumes a pendulum pattern (Inner, Middle, Outer, Middle) rather than a continuous cyclic reset.
tip: Check if boundary-reaching patterns bounce back or wrap around to the start.

question: Problem Description: A round Roti is divided into 8 equal slices by lines passing through its center. In figure 1, only the slice at the 12 o'clock position is shaded. In figure 2, the 12 o'clock and 1:30 positions are shaded. In figure 3, the 12, 1:30, and 3 o'clock positions are shaded. What will be the next figure in the series?

tip: Differentiate between an element moving vs an area expanding via additive shading.

question: Problem Description: A vertical ladder (Seedi) is drawn with 5 rungs. In figure 1, a small bucket hangs on the lowest rung (rung 1) on the far left side. In figure 2, the bucket is on the second rung up, but hanging on the far right side. In figure 3, the bucket is on the third rung up, back on the left side. answer: Option D: The bucket is on the fourth rung, right side.
explanation: There are two concurrent rules. Rule 1: The bucket translates vertically upward by exactly one rung each step (1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4). Rule 2: The bucket alternates horizontally between the left and right sides (Left -> Right -> Left -> Right).
trick: Option B correctly applies the vertical ascent but forgets to toggle the horizontal position.
tip: Isolate horizontal toggles from vertical translations in grid-like structures.

question: Problem Description: A zigzag line resembling a slithering snake has 3 upward-pointing peaks. In figure 1, all 3 peaks are sharp, angular points. explanation: The transformation from 'sharp' to 'rounded' is applied sequentially from left to right, accumulating in each step. The logical next step is to apply the transformation to the final remaining sharp peak.
trick: Option A assumes the transformation moves rather than accumulates.
tip: Sequential accumulation changes an object permanently from left to right.

question: Problem Description: A sequence of Diwali lanterns (Kandeel) is shown. Figure 1 shows a central triangular body (3 sides) with 1 decorative tassel hanging below it. Figure 2 shows a square body (4 sides) with 2 hanging tassels. Figure 3 shows a pentagonal body (5 sides) with 3 hanging tassels. What will be the next figure in the series?

trick: Option C correctly updates the central polygon but fails to increment the number of tassels.
tip: Count the sub-elements (tassels, sides) and establish their parallel number sequences.

question: Problem Description: A top-down view of a Marigold (Genda) flower shows 4 concentric rings of petals surrounding a central pollen dot. In figure 1, all 4 rings are fully drawn. answer: Option B: Only the outermost, largest ring of petals remains.
explanation: The rings of petals are being sequentially deleted one by one from the inside out. Following this pattern, the 3rd ring from the center is deleted next, leaving only the 4th (outermost) ring.
trick: Option C deletes the center dot, which breaks the established pattern of deleting petal rings.
tip: Deletion patterns often follow a strict directional path (inside-out, top-bottom).

question: Problem Description: A kite is flying with a trailing string. In figure 1, the kite points directly East, and its string has 1 tied knot. In figure 2, the kite points North, and the string has 3 tied knots. In figure 3, the kite points West, and the string has 5 tied knots. What will be the next figure in the series?

trick: Option A applies the correct rotation but miscalculates the knot addition as +1 instead of +2.
tip: Check for odd/even numerical progressions in element counting.

question: Problem Description: A square Carrom board has a striker. In figure 1, the striker is at the exact center of the bottom edge. In figure 2, it is at the exact center of the left edge. In figure 3, it is at the exact center of the top edge. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The striker is in the exact center of the right edge.

explanation: The striker translates from mid-edge to mid-edge in a 90-degree clockwise sequence around the perimeter of the board: Bottom -> Left -> Top. The next 90-degree clockwise translation places it at the right edge.
trick: Option D suggests the striker moves inwards, abandoning the perimeter translation rule.
tip: Perimeter movements on a square from edge to edge are 90-degree translations.

question: Problem Description: A square window frame is being filled with a metal grill (Jaali). In figure 1, there is a single vertical iron bar cutting the square exactly in half. In figure 2, a single horizontal bar is added, intersecting the vertical bar perfectly in the center to form a cross (+). Option B: A second horizontal bar is added, creating a tic-tac-toe/hashtag grid (#).

answer: Option B: A second horizontal bar is added, creating a tic-tac-toe/hashtag grid (#).
explanation: The series alternates adding bars by their orientation to maintain structural balance: vertical, then horizontal, then vertical. To continue the alternating sequence, the next addition must be a horizontal bar.
trick: Option C breaks the orthogonal (vertical/horizontal) pattern by introducing a diagonal line.
tip: Sequential construction often alternates axes (X, then Y, then X) for stability.

question: Problem Description: A ceiling fan (Pankha) is viewed from directly below. In figure 1, it has a central hub and 1 blade pointing directly North. In figure 2, a second blade is added pointing directly South, forming a straight line. In figure 3, a third blade is added, and all 3 blades are now spaced evenly apart (120 degrees). answer: Option B: A fourth blade is added, spaced evenly 90 degrees apart like a plus sign (+).
explanation: The sequence incrementally adds one fan blade per step. Crucially, the configuration dynamically re-adjusts every time to maintain perfect radial symmetry. 2 blades = 180° apart. 3 blades = 120° apart. 4 blades = 90° apart.
trick: Option A adds the correct number of blades but ignores the dynamic symmetry rule.
tip: Observe if added elements force existing elements to shift to maintain equilibrium.

question: Problem Description: A 3x3 square grid is drawn. In figure 1, the square in the top-left corner is shaded black. In figure 2, the shaded square moves one space to the right (top-middle) and changes color to grey. In figure 3, it moves one more space to the right (top-right) and changes back to black. answer: Option B: The shaded square wraps around to the left side of the middle row and turns grey.
explanation: The shaded square translates through the grid exactly like reading a book (left to right, top to bottom). After hitting the end of row 1, it wraps to the start of row 2. Additionally, the color strictly toggles between black and grey in each step.
trick: Option C implies a bouncing pendulum movement, which contradicts standard grid wrap-around reading logic.
tip: Grid movements reaching an edge frequently wrap around to the next row.

question: Problem Description: A ball of dough (Aata) is flattened. In figure 1, it is a perfect circle. In figure 2, it is stretched sideways into a wide, horizontal oval. In figure 3, it is compressed horizontally and stretched vertically into a tall oval. In figure 4, it is stretched back into a wide, horizontal oval. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: A very large perfect circle.

answer: Option C: A tall, vertical oval.
explanation: After the initial circular shape, the dough toggles back and forth between two strict states: a horizontal stretch and a vertical stretch. Since figure 4 is a horizontal oval, figure 5 must toggle back to a tall, vertical oval.
trick: Option A assumes the sequence circles back to the very first starting frame, rather than continuing the established A-B-A-B toggle.
tip: Exclude the 'start state' when determining continuous toggling sequences.

question: Problem Description: A visual sequence shows the phases of the moon (Chand). In figure 1, it is a thin white crescent curving along the right edge. In figure 2, the white area expands to form an exact half-moon (the right half is illuminated). In figure 3, it expands further to a gibbous moon (mostly white, with a sliver of dark on the far left). What will be the next figure in the series?

explanation: The illuminated white area is steadily and continuously expanding from right to left across the circle in each step. The logical completion of this expansion covers the remaining dark sliver, resulting in a fully illuminated circle.
trick: Option A breaks the continuous forward momentum by jumping straight to a reset state.
tip: Continuous directional growth naturally builds toward a fully completed shape.

question: Problem Description: A 6-pointed Star of David (two overlapping triangles) has a small Diya placed on one of its outer points. In figure 1, the Diya is on the top-most point. In figure 2, it moves clockwise to the immediately adjacent point (skipping 0 points). In figure 3, it moves clockwise, skipping exactly 1 point, to land on the bottom-most point. Option D: It moves clockwise, skipping 3 points, to land back on the top-most point.

explanation: The number of outer points skipped between jumps increases by 1 each time. Jump 1 skips 0 points. Jump 2 skips 1 point. Jump 3 must skip 2 points. From the bottom point, skipping the bottom-left and the mid-left lands the Diya on the top-left point.
trick: Option B assumes the skip distance freezes at 1 instead of continuing to accelerate.
tip: Look for accelerating movement patterns by counting the unvisited spaces between jumps.

question: Problem Description: Three identical squares are stacked vertically, resembling a traffic light. In figure 1, only the top square is filled with a black crosshatch pattern. In figure 2, the top and middle squares are filled. In figure 3, only the middle square is filled. In figure 4, the middle and bottom squares are filled. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: All three squares are filled.
Option B: Only the bottom square is filled.
Option C: The top and bottom squares are filled.
Option D: Only the top square is filled.
answer: Option B: Only the bottom square is filled.
explanation: The visual is an 'inchworm' or cascading downward movement. The fill expands downward by one square, then contracts downward by one square. Top -> Top+Mid -> Mid -> Mid+Bot. The next step is contracting downward, leaving only the Bottom square filled.
trick: Option A assumes standard cumulative addition, missing the alternating expand/contract logic of the 'inchworm' movement.

question: Problem Description: A regular hexagon contains a small arrow pointing to one of its six corners. In figure 1, the arrow points to the top-most corner and is colored black. In figure 2, the arrow points to the top-right corner and is colored white. In figure 3, the arrow points to the bottom-right corner and is colored black. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: The arrow points to the bottom-most corner and is colored white.
Option B: The arrow points to the bottom-most corner and is colored black.
Option C: The arrow points to the bottom-left corner and is colored white.

answer: Option A: The arrow points to the bottom-most corner and is colored white.
explanation: Rule 1: The arrow rotates exactly 60 degrees (one corner) clockwise in each step. Top -> Top-Right -> Bottom-Right -> Bottom. Rule 2: The arrow's color strictly toggles between black and white in each step. Black -> White -> Black -> White.
trick: Option B correctly tracks the rotation but forgets to toggle the color to white.
tip: Check the status of every variable attribute (position, angle, color) independently.

question: Problem Description: A traditional weighing scale (Taraju) has two hanging pans. In figure 1, the left pan holds a Triangle (3 sides), and the right pan holds a Square (4 sides). answer: Option A: Left pan holds a Hexagon (6 sides), Right pan holds a Heptagon (7 sides).

tip: Ignore real-world functional goals if a strict mathematical or geometric pattern is established.

question: Problem Description: A 6-pointed Star of David (Rangoli base) is drawn using 6 small overlapping triangles. In figure 1, all 6 outer points (triangles) are present. answer: Option B: The bottom-left point is deleted.
explanation: The deletion sequence targets pairs of polar opposites. First, it deleted the Top, then its opposite, the Bottom. Next, it deleted the Top-Right. Following the established pattern, it must immediately delete its exact polar opposite, which is the Bottom-Left point.
trick: Option A assumes a simple clockwise deletion (Top-Right, then Bottom-Right) ignoring the established polar-opposite pairing.
tip: Deletions across a central axis usually occur in opposing pairs.

question: Problem Description: A pair of tailor's scissors (Kainchi) is shown. In figure 1, the blades are completely closed, forming a 0-degree angle. question: Problem Description: A 2x2 grid contains 4 distinct symbols: a Sun, a Moon, a Star, and a Cloud. question: Problem Description: A drawing represents the branching roots of a Banyan tree. In figure 1, there is a single straight vertical root line. options: Option A: The endpoints split again, creating 6 total endpoints.

answer: Option B: The endpoints split again, creating 8 total endpoints.
explanation: The branching mechanism represents an exponential geometric progression where every single existing endpoint multiplies by 2 in each step. The sequence of endpoints is 1 -> 2 -> 4. The next step must be 4 * 2 = 8 endpoints.
trick: Option A treats the growth as a simple arithmetic addition (+2) rather than an exponential geometric split (x2).
tip: Fractal or branching patterns usually represent geometric multiplication, not simple addition.

question: Problem Description: A horizontal sliding track has 3 distinct slots: Left, Middle, and Right. There are two blocks: one Black, one White. In figure 1, the Black block is in the Left slot, the White is in the Middle, and the Right slot is empty. In figure 2, the Black block is in the Left slot, the Middle is empty, and the White block is in the Right slot. In figure 3, the Left slot is empty, the Black block is in the Middle, and the White block is in the Right slot. What will be the next figure in the series?
options: Option A: Black in the Middle, White in the Left, Right empty.
Option B: Black in the Right, White in the Left, Middle empty.
Option C: Black in the Left, White in the Middle, Right empty.
Option D: Black in the Middle, White in the Middle, Left and Right empty.
answer: Option C: Black in the Left, White in the Middle, Right empty.
explanation: This is a sequence of alternating individual moves. Step 1 to 2: The White block moves right into the empty slot. Step 2 to 3: The Black block moves right into the newly empty middle slot. Step 3 to 4: Since they can't move right anymore, the pattern resets or loops. Actually, look at the empty space moving left! Empty space: Right (Fig 1) -> Mid (Fig 2) -> Left (Fig 3). The empty space simply slides left one position at a time. Therefore, in the next step, the empty space loops back to the Right slot. This pushes Black back to Left, and White back to Middle.
trick: Option A assumes the blocks leapfrog over each other, but sliding puzzles only allow movement into adjacent empty spaces.
tip: In sliding block puzzles, tracking the movement of the 'empty space' is often easier than tracking the blocks.

question: Problem Description: Two hands of a clock are shown. In figure 1, both the long Minute hand and the short Hour hand point exactly to 12 o'clock. tip: When realistic objects are used, verify if they are following their actual real-world mechanical rules.

question: Problem Description: A rubber band is stretched tightly over a pegboard. In figure 1, it is stretched over 3 pegs, forming a triangle. answer: Option A: A side is pulled out to form a 6-sided hexagon.

question: Problem Description: A visual sequence of barefoot footprints (resembling walking) is shown on the ground. In figure 1, a single Left footprint is pointing North. question: Problem Description: A red Onion (Pyaaz) is sliced in half, showing 5 concentric, nested arc layers. In figure 1, all 5 layers are perfectly intact. tip: Track alternating patterns of deletion on symmetrical objects.

question: Problem Description: A horizontal line represents the horizon over the ocean. In figure 1, a full circular Sun is completely above the line. In figure 2, the Sun translates straight down so it is exactly half-submerged below the line (a semi-circle is visible). In figure 3, the Sun has translated completely below the line and is entirely invisible. In figure 4, a crescent Moon translates straight up, appearing half-risen above the line. options: Option A: The Moon translates completely above the line.
Option B: The Moon translates back down below the line.
Option C: The Sun rises again instantly.

answer: Option A: The Moon translates completely above the line.
explanation: The sequence models a continuous vertical translation (setting and rising) through three positional states: Fully Above -> Half Submerged -> Fully Below. The Sun goes Above -> Half -> Below. The Moon is doing the reverse (rising): Below (invisible in fig 3 alongside the sun) -> Half Above (fig 4) -> Fully Above.
trick: Option D changes the shape of the object (crescent to full) instead of continuing its established spatial translation.
tip: Objects entering a frame often follow the exact same translation distance/speed rules as objects that just exited.
